analysis.one_liner: Permanently funds water and sewer repairs, lead pipe and PFAS cleanup, and blocks privatized water systems from federal aid.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without ever getting a vote; it would have directed about $34.9 billion a year in federal money to water and sewer infrastructure.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have moved roughly $35 billion a year from the Treasury to water and sewer programs every year without a new vote of Congress — funding repairs of public water systems, replacement of lead pipes, cleanup of PFAS contamination, septic system repairs for homeowners, safe drinking water at schools, and rural water wells. It would have restricted federal revolving loan funds to publicly owned water systems and allowed communities to buy private water companies into public ownership. It also required American-made materials and union-standard wages on funded projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that drink from public water systems — especially people with lead service lines, PFAS-contaminated wells, or failing septic systems — would get federally funded repairs and filters. Rural communities, tribes, and schools would get dedicated grants. Construction workers would get prevailing-wage jobs on large public projects. Water ratepayers would benefit because federal money reduces the repair costs that otherwise flow into water bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with unsafe or unaffordable water

how_it_helps.text: Sends $18.1 billion a year to clean water programs and $16.4 billion a year to drinking water programs, including capitalization grants for state revolving loan funds, without requiring a new appropriation each year [S3].

Creates a grant program to pay for repairing, replacing, or upgrading homeowners' septic tanks and drainage fields, and makes permanent a grant program for household water well systems in rural areas at $348.5 million a year [S2] [S3].
Expands school drinking water grants from $5 million to $1.05 billion a year to make school fountains, coolers, and bottle-filling stations lead free [S3].

Lets state revolving funds pay to replace lead service lines on private property, help public water systems switch sources or upgrade treatment after PFAS contamination, and buy filtration systems for contaminated household wells [S3].

Restricts federal drinking water loans to publicly owned, operated, and managed water systems, and makes funds available to purchase private water systems from willing sellers to bring them into public ownership — ending the use of federal money to support privatized water [S3].
Requires states to allow and use project labor agreements, preserves prevailing wage requirements, and mandates American-made iron, steel, and manufactured products in drinking water projects [S3].

Directs the EPA to study water affordability nationwide, water shutoffs for unpaid bills, and discriminatory practices by water providers, with a report and recommendations to Congress within one year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund about $34.9 billion every year through automatic Treasury transfers that bypass the normal annual appropriations process [S3]. Nonunion construction contractors would face project labor agreements and prevailing wage rules on funded work [S3]. Private water companies would lose access to federal revolving loan funds and could be bought out into public ownership with those funds [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and private water companies

drawbacks.text: The bill creates permanent, automatic spending of roughly $34.9 billion a year that transfers from the Treasury on October 1 each year without further appropriation or fiscal year limitation, removing the annual congressional review that most programs receive [S3].

Project labor agreements and prevailing wage requirements raise construction costs relative to open bidding, and Buy American rules can raise material costs and delay projects; supporters accept these as the price of wage standards and domestic manufacturing [S3].

Restricting revolving fund assistance to publicly owned systems takes away a financing tool that some small towns used for privately run systems, though the bill allows an exception for small systems serving fewer than 10,000 people [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have put a very large, steady federal investment into water systems that communities cannot afford to fix on their own, aimed directly at health problems — lead, PFAS, failing septic systems — and at rate affordability. The costs are real: a large permanent federal commitment outside the normal budget process, somewhat higher construction costs from labor and sourcing rules, and the exclusion of private water companies from federal financing. It was an ambitious spending bill whose price and design invited opposition; its flaw was not hidden but its path through Congress was.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on February 28, 2019, and the committee never acted on it; it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
Three Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no other action was ever taken on it [S4] [S5].
The committee held no markup, reported no version, and the full Senate never voted on it during the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers avoided a new automatic $35 billion-a-year commitment, and private water companies kept access to a market that the bill would have closed off. Communities with lead pipes, PFAS-contaminated wells, or unaffordable water bills got no federal help from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited three Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-lead at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by an Independent and cosponsored only by three Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and a Republican-majority committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar most privately owned water systems from federal revolving fund assistance and allow communities to use those funds to buy private systems into public ownership, shrinking the market for investor-owned water companies. Its restriction to publicly owned systems runs against private companies' interest in keeping and expanding their customer base.

Roughly $35 billion a year in funded projects would mean a large, steady pipeline of construction work. Prevailing wage and project labor agreement requirements would steer that work toward union-standard labor practices.

industries.industry: Plumbing manufacturers and septic and well service companies
industries.note: Lead pipe replacement grants, school drinking water upgrades, septic system grants, and rural well funding create demand for pipes, fixtures, filtration systems, and septic and well contractors. Buy American rules direct that demand to domestic manufacturers.

industries.industry: Households with private wells and septic systems
industries.note: New grant programs would pay directly for septic repairs and contaminated-well filtration, replacing costs those homeowners currently bear alone.
